sections.authorBiography: Frank R. Stockton was born in Philadelphia on 5 April 1834. He worked as a wood engraver before turning to writing, and became assistant editor of St. Nicholas, the leading American children's magazine. He wrote fairy tales and comic stories, and his puzzle story "The Lady, or the Tiger?" (1882) made him famous; readers wrote to him for decades asking for the answer, which he never gave. He died on 20 April 1902.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Which came out of the opened door,—the lady, or the tiger” slowly and put it in my own words: The narrator asks which came out of the door: the lady or the tiger. Next, craft. I notice it is an unanswered question, so the ending is handed to the reader. The strongest word is “tiger”: the plain, dangerous animal stands against "the lady," so the choice is death or a rival's marriage. Then, effect. Why does the story end on this question? My answer: Stockton refuses to tell us, so we must decide what the princess's jealousy and love would do; the reader becomes the judge.

segments.script: Stockton first read this story aloud at a party in 1882 before printing it in The Century magazine that November, and readers wrote to Stockton demanding the answer. strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Lady, or the Tiger?.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Lady, or the Tiger?: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the story to jealousy and love.
